opus-5.5.text:
I'm actually very bullish on it, and I think it's one of the most important directions for the whole industry. If you look at how most companies build with AI today, the model is kind of frozen. You pick a foundation model, maybe you fine-tune it once, you ship it, and then it just sits there while your product, your users, and your data keep evolving. That's a mismatch. The application is alive, but the model isn't.

What we see with the developers we work with is that the real differentiation doesn't come from the base model. Everyone has access to roughly the same open models and the same closed APIs. The differentiation comes from the data flywheel inside the product: how users interact, what they accept, what they edit, what they reject, where the model fails. That signal is incredibly valuable, and right now most of it is thrown away or only used offline months later.

So the vision is a closed loop. You serve the model, you capture feedback, explicit like thumbs up and down or implicit like whether a code suggestion was kept, you turn that into training signal through fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, and you roll out an improved model, ideally continuously. Over time the model becomes specialized to your use case in a way nobody else can replicate, because nobody else has your users and your data.

That said, I don't want to oversimplify, because there are real challenges. The first is signal quality. User feedback is noisy, sparse, and sometimes adversarial, so you need good ways to filter it, build reward models, and avoid overfitting to a vocal minority. The second is safety and stability. You don't want to update a model and suddenly regress on things that used to work, so you need strong evaluation, versioning, and the ability to A/B test and roll back. The third is infrastructure. Doing this continuously means training and inference need to be tightly integrated. You can't have a six-week cycle of exporting data, training somewhere else, and redeploying. It has to be fast, cheap, and automated.

That's a big part of why we think about this as a platform problem rather than just a modeling problem. If the friction of the loop is high, people won't do it. If you make it nearly seamless, where serving, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment all live together, then continuous improvement becomes the default rather than a heroic research project.

So my view is this is where things are headed. The winning AI applications won't be the ones that picked the best model on day one. They'll be the ones whose models get better every single day because they learn from their own users.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's really where the whole industry is heading. When we started Fireworks, the thesis was that inference is not just a serving problem, it's actually the beginning of a loop. You deploy a model, real users interact with it, and that interaction generates signal that no pretraining dataset could ever give you. The question is how fast and how safely you can close that loop.

My view is that continuous training on live feedback is inevitable, but the naive version of it is dangerous. If you just take raw user interactions and keep pushing gradient updates into a production model, you get drift, you get reward hacking, you get the model optimizing for whatever proxy you measured instead of what the user actually wanted. We saw versions of this with recommendation systems years ago. So I don't think of it as the model literally learning in the request path.

What I think works is a tighter but still staged loop. You collect the feedback, both explicit, like thumbs up or down, and implicit, like did the user accept the code, did they rephrase the question, did they abandon the session. You use that to build evaluation sets and preference data. Then you do targeted fine-tuning, often with reinforcement fine-tuning, on a smaller specialized model, and you validate it against the evals before it ever takes production traffic. The cadence can be days or even hours instead of months, which already feels continuous from the application developer's perspective, but there is still a gate.

The other piece is that this changes what the ideal production model looks like. For a long time the assumption was you want the biggest, most general frontier model. But once you have a feedback loop, a smaller model that is tuned on your actual traffic will often beat a larger generic one on quality, and it's much cheaper and faster to serve. That's the compounding advantage. The data moat is really an inference moat, because the people who serve the most traffic have the most signal.

So I'm very bullish on it. I just think the winners will be the ones who build the evaluation and safety infrastructure around the loop, not the ones who move fastest at updating weights.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there, because once a model is in a real application, you start to see the gap between what you trained it to do and what users actually need. That feedback can help you close the gap.

But I would separate continuously collecting feedback from continuously updating the model. User feedback is noisy. If someone accepts an answer, that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s correct. So you need a way to understand those signals, evaluate whether an update actually improves the model, and catch regressions before exposing more users to it.

To me, the exciting opportunity is building that learning loop: the application gets better through use, but you still have control over what it learns and how those changes reach users.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very promising direction, because once a model is in an application, that’s where you learn whether it’s actually useful. But there’s a big difference between collecting feedback continuously and updating the model continuously.

User feedback can be noisy. If someone clicks on an answer, does that mean it was correct, or just that it was interesting? And different users may want different things. So you need to understand what signal you’re collecting before you use it to change the model.

I would start with a controlled feedback loop: collect those signals, evaluate potential improvements, and then roll out updates with monitoring and the ability to roll back. Some feedback might be better handled through personalization or updating the information the model retrieves, rather than changing the model itself.

So I’m optimistic about applications that keep learning from their users. The challenge is making sure that learning produces a measurable improvement while preserving reliability and user privacy.
